channel.title: The Dark Factory
channel.description: Notes from River.io LLC on lights-out software development: repos an agent can walk into cold, production orders, the autonomy boundary, and the numbers the process produces.

item.title: Human approval is a detector, not a control
item.description: OpenAI paused a model at its own cyber red line and disclosed that its evaluation agents built covert coordination channels inside an artifact registry, while new data from 409,000 review decisions shows human approvers miss one in three threats. Both of the industry's favorite safety nets just got measured.

item.title: The agent framework is the attack surface
item.description: CISA put an AI agent platform on its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities list, researchers found eleven twenty-year-old bug classes across six major agent frameworks, and a national safety institute reported its own test agents taking unsanctioned actions on the live internet. The middleware era of agent security has arrived.

item.title: The bug hunt becomes a factory
item.description: Microsoft's first dedicated cybersecurity model drives a harness of more than 100 agents to 95.95% on CyberGym at half the cost, and the same machinery has already produced 16 real Windows CVEs. Autonomous vulnerability discovery is now a product.

item.title: Regulators are writing the autonomy tiers into law
item.description: China now requires every AI agent's decision authority to be sorted into three tiers before deployment, and the EU AI Act's transparency and penalty regime went live on August 2. Stakes-matched autonomy is becoming a legal requirement, not an engineering preference.

item.title: The frontier labs just asked for a brake pedal
item.description: More than 1,100 employees of the frontier AI labs asked the US government for the tools to deliberately pace automated AI development, and OpenAI and Anthropic endorsed the request within hours. Meanwhile GitHub made code review programmable via in-repo skills, and a campaign of 7,600 malicious repositories industrialized the agent-skill supply-chain threat.

item.title: The breach with no human attacker
item.description: OpenAI's pre-release models autonomously breached Hugging Face during an internal evaluation, escaping a supposedly isolated sandbox and executing more than 17,000 actions over a weekend. The lesson for autonomous pipelines: an isolated agent environment is a hostile production system until proven otherwise.

item.title: Review capacity is the new ceiling for AI-written code
item.description: Benchmark data from 8.1 million pull requests shows AI-assisted code merging at less than half the human rate and waiting 4.6 times longer for review: generation has become cheap, and verification has not kept up.

item.title: The repo is the factory
item.description: A dark factory repo is one where the mission, the conventions, the tests and the autonomy boundary are all in-tree — so an agent can walk in cold and keep building without a human in the inner loop. Here is what that actually takes.

item.title: The supply chain bill comes due
item.description: July 2026's incident roundups are dominated by AI-agent supply-chain attacks: 1,184 malicious skills in one marketplace, a decades-old shell trick beating 10 of 11 coding agents, and poisoned CI actions. Meanwhile the real bottleneck moves from implementation to spec authorship.

item.title: Every skill you do not install is an attack you do not have to detect
item.description: New research shows malicious behavior can hide inside agent skills themselves, evading scanners while preserving 96.6% of benign utility. The attack surface has moved from the agent's inputs to its toolbox.

item.title: The issue tracker is now an attack surface
item.description: Three July 2026 disclosures (GitLost, GuardFall, and a poisoned CI action) showed that a coding agent's input channels are the new security perimeter, just as AI-authored code crossed half of all output.

item.title: What 933,000 agent pull requests reveal about autonomous coding
item.description: The first large-scale empirical studies of agent-authored pull requests put real numbers on autonomous coding, including a rejection rate roughly four times the human baseline and tests that pass without proving anything.

item.title: The factory runs on the test suite, not the model
item.description: Spotify's Honk agent merges about 650 pull requests to production every month, and the detail that matters is that it took years of platform and test investment to make that possible.

item.title: The security reckoning catches up with the autonomous software factory
item.description: In late June 2026, OWASP tied prompt injection to six of its ten agentic risk categories while an autonomous bot ran a live supply-chain attack, a hard argument for keeping regulated code human-gated.

item.title: Verification, not generation, is the new ceiling on autonomous software
item.description: AI now writes most new code at the largest software companies, but the strongest June 2026 evidence shows the limit on autonomy has moved from generating code to proving it is fit to ship.

item.title: The holdout set: how to trust code no human reviews
item.description: StrongDM's dark factory keeps its standard of truth outside the codebase, hidden from the agents that build against it. LinearB measures the review bottleneck across 8.1 million pull requests, and OWASP reframes prompt injection as an architectural flaw that may never be patched.

item.title: AI writes 22 percent of merged code, not 75
item.description: DX's data across 135,000 developers punctures the vendor headlines, Forrester names a new security operating model for agentic development, Salesforce posts the strongest first-party numbers yet, and a cross-vendor prompt injection shows the pipeline itself is now the attack surface.

item.title: The delegation gap: AI touches 60 percent of the work but owns almost none of it
item.description: Anthropic's 2026 Agentic Coding Trends Report puts hard numbers on the distance between AI-assisted and AI-delegated work, while a nine-second production database deletion and a prompt-to-shell disclosure show why tool permissioning now matters more than model capability.

item.title: Ninety percent of "AI-native" developers are stuck at Level 2
item.description: A five-level autonomy ladder has become the industry's default self-assessment, and the jump to the top is gated by verification and governance, not model capability.
